name: Manor of Cardross
summary: The manor house on the lower Clyde that Robert the Bruce built for himself after the wars, and where he died on 7 June 1329 — a hunting lodge rather than a castle, and no longer standing.
overview: The Manor of Cardross was a royal residence near the River Clyde associated with Robert the Bruce’s final years.
Bruce died there in 1329 after securing a stronger Scottish monarchy.
knownFor: Death of Robert the Bruce on 7 June 1329
A manerium built for the king in the late 1320s, not a castle
Its site disputed between Mains of Cardross on the Leven and Castlehill
Recorded in the Exchequer Rolls of Scotland rather than in stone

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Cardross near the Clyde estuary in Scotland was a royal manor where Robert the Bruce spent his final years and died in June 1329. The manor was his preferred residence during his last period of illness.

It is the one royal house in this archive that a visitor cannot see at all. Nothing of it survives above ground, its exact site is argued over, and everything known about the building comes from the crown’s account rolls rather than from its remains.

contentSections.title: Where the manor stood
paragraphs: The parish of Cardross in the Middle Ages was larger than the village that carries the name today, and the two are not the same place. Bruce bought the lands of Pillanflatt, on the western bank of the River Leven, from the Earl of Lennox in 1326, and the park attached to his house took in those lands.

The weight of scholarship therefore puts the manor a few kilometres east of Cardross village, on the Leven near the field still called the Mains of Cardross, south of Renton. The older tradition placed it at Castlehill, further west, but that rests on little: the accounts show the king keeping boats and a ship by his house, which suits a site on the river rather than an inland hill. Neither identification has been settled by excavation, and the Mains name is evidence of the area rather than proof of the spot.

contentSections.title: The house the king built
paragraphs: The crown’s records call it a manerium, a manor house, and never a castle or a palace — a distinction the clerks kept carefully. From the expenses entered in the Exchequer Rolls it appears to have been a single-storey building with a hall, a chapel, glazed windows and a thatched roof, with a park, a garden, falcons and a hunting establishment attached.

In modern terms it was a hunting lodge, built for a man in his fifties who had spent twenty years in the field and wanted a quiet house by the water rather than another fortress. The king who had taken English-held castles by escalade and then slighted them so they could not be used against him chose not to build one for himself.

contentSections.title: The king’s last years
paragraphs: Bruce retired to Cardross after the fighting ended and the settlement was made. The Declaration of Arbroath had been sent to the pope in 1320, and the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton of 1328 brought English recognition of Scottish independence and of his title as king.

He was ill through those years, with a disease the sources do not identify precisely; leprosy is the traditional diagnosis and is not supported by anything in the record. He sailed on the Clyde, kept his falcons, and governed from the house.

contentSections.title: Death and dispersal, 1329
paragraphs: Robert the Bruce died at the manor on 7 June 1329, aged fifty-four. His body was carried across Scotland to Dunfermline Abbey and buried in the choir among the kings.

Robert’s death at Cardross ended the reign of the king who had secured Scottish independence through the Declaration of Arbroath (1320) and the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton (1328), by which England recognized Scottish sovereignty. His heart was removed after death and taken on crusade by James Douglas, part of a tradition of vow-fulfillment by proxy. Douglas was killed fighting the Moors in Spain, and the heart was brought home and buried at Melrose Abbey.
